sample_n: NR (Table 1 person-time sample sizes not in excerpt)
exposure: Traffic noise at two levels (low 55.6 dBA vs high 70.5 dBA, at least 10 dB apart) crossed with lilac (Syringa amurensis) plant odour concentration graded none to strong on a 7-point scale
behaviour_measure: Crowd walking path (lateral position of the trajectory relative to the noise and odour sources) and crowd walking speed in m/s, extracted from drone observation video
key_finding: At high SPL pedestrian paths shifted away from the traffic-noise side and moved up to about 0.3 m toward the odour source as odour strengthened, and mean crowd speed slowed from 1.24 m/s to 1.18 m/s, whereas path and speed were almost unaffected at low SPL
effect_stats: max longitudinal path shift about 0.3 m; mean speed 1.24 m/s to 1.18 m/s at high SPL; overall mean 1.17 m/s; repeated measures ANOVA in Tables 2-3 with F and p values not in excerpt

exposure: Street-segment traffic noise level, with air quality index, Green View Index, NDVI, blue space density, slope, Floor Area Ratio, connectivity and traffic accidents as co-exposures
behaviour_measure: Running intensity per street segment, computed as total length of Strava GPS running routes within a 20 m buffer divided by buffer area (range 0.001-3.45 m/m2)
key_finding: Running intensity was positively correlated with traffic noise and air pollution and negatively with urban density, connectivity and traffic accidents, while blue space density was the predominant positive predictor
effect_stats: NR (multilevel model coefficients reported in Table 2, values not in excerpt)

sample_n: NR (number of walk-along participants with psychosis not stated in excerpt)
exposure: Naturally occurring urban street sounds and noise during walk-alongs, including short and very loud metallic noises near a parked truck, a car horn and a strident tyre screech
behaviour_measure: Video-coded embodied and verbal conduct while walking: gaze reorientation and looking down, orienting to the noise source, walking away from the partner and solitary gait, turn-taking (minimal and delayed replies, absence of topic initiation) and silences
key_finding: Loud strident street noises were followed by observable disengagement in the participant with psychosis: gaze aversion and orienting toward the noise source, progressively walking away from the partner and minimal or delayed conversational contributions including a 29-second silence, the longest of the entire walk-along

sample_n: 262 valid questionnaires (273 collected of 300 distributed; 10 soundwalk sampling points)
exposure: Musical theme landscape combined with the site soundscape at Feicui Lake scenic spot (musical fountain, violin island, natural and artificial sounds), with LAeq measured by sound level meter along the violin island walkway
behaviour_measure: Reported staying behaviour at the scenic spot (viewing the scenery or resting), captured through the soundwalk and Likert-scale questionnaire
key_finding: Musical theme landscape and soundscape were reported to affect visitors emotions at the individual level and their behaviours such as staying to view the scenery or rest at the social level, but no quantified behavioural outcome is given in the excerpt

exposure: Seven laboratory auditory environments combining 68 dB traffic noise with residential activity sounds or commercial activity sounds at varying signal-to-noise ratios representing low and high activity intensity (field LAeq: TN 68.3, RS 66.2, CS 67.8 dBA)
behaviour_measure: Human activity spatial context operationalised as activity type (commuting, residential, commercial) and activity intensity (SNR of activity sounds over traffic noise); no behaviour was observed on participants
key_finding: Adding human activity sounds to constant traffic noise lowered the perceived dominance of traffic noise and raised acoustic comfort despite higher acoustic energy, with best comfort for low-intensity residential and high-intensity commercial activity and more actively engaging soundscapes at higher activity intensity
effect_stats: NR (repeated measures ANOVA reported in Tables 2-5, values not in excerpt)

sample_n: 81,403 Strava cycle trips plus 335 surveyed cyclists
exposure: Road traffic noise exposure in Dublin estimated from local environmental data and 17 noise monitoring stations (WHO 53 dB Lden limit cited; cyclist levels reported at 71-75 dB)
behaviour_measure: Self-reported temporal and spatial detours taken because of noise, plus Strava-recorded cycling route choice and trip volumes for a direct route versus the popular detour route
key_finding: Cyclists reported that noise changed their behaviour mainly through temporal and spatial detours, and the popular detour route carried about 10 dB(A) lower noise exposure than the direct route at the cost of roughly 4 extra minutes
effect_stats: +10 dB(A) exposure increase on the direct route versus the popular detour, for a saving of approximately 4 min; survey percentages in Table 2 not in excerpt

exposure: Urban park acoustic environment: LAeq measured for 10 min at each sampling site plus identified sound sources (traffic noise, music, human sounds, natural sounds) across fitness trails, open squares, tree-shaded squares and pavilions
behaviour_measure: Behavioural state of each respondent classified as sitting, walking or acoustic behaviour and sustained for over 15 min, recorded by both observation and questioning
key_finding: Respondents in different behavioural states (sitting, walking, acoustic) reported different acoustic-visual perceptions and satisfaction, so behavioural state conditioned soundscape evaluation and predicted acoustic, visual and overall satisfaction
effect_stats: NR (multiple linear regression results in Tables 4-6, values not in excerpt)

sample_n: 355 small-medium public parks (359 when all parks included), Queens, New York City
exposure: Park noise level as one of 12 social and environmental predictors, alongside park area, canopy cover, percent water and impervious cover, distance to public transportation, summer mean temperature, median income and ethnic diversity
behaviour_measure: iNaturalist citizen-science records per park: number of Observers, number of Observations, Observed Biodiversity and a calculated Interaction metric (users x observations)
key_finding: For small-medium parks all four nature-interaction metrics were significantly influenced by noise together with park area, canopy cover, blood pressure and asthma prevalence and summer mean temperature; the sign and magnitude of the noise coefficient are not given in the excerpt
effect_stats: NR (GLM estimates, standard deviations, P values and McFadden pseudo-R2 in Tables 3-4, values not in excerpt)

sample_n: NR (residents video-recorded at two community activity spaces; count not in excerpt)
exposure: Loudspeaker sound interventions in two community outdoor activity spaces: mixed birdsong, water sound, traffic noise and construction noise, all equalised in SPL, plus a quiet control condition
behaviour_measure: Video-coded social interaction indicators: social participation for paired and grouped interactions (SP), occurrence of brief and prolonged social interactions (OSI-B, OSI-P) and depth of social interactions (DSI)
key_finding: A more natural community sound environment increased social interaction: birdsong raised paired social interactions by 16.3 percent versus traffic noise and water sound raised grouped social interactions by 16.6 percent versus the control
effect_stats: paired social interactions +16.3% (birdsong vs traffic noise); grouped social interactions +16.6% (water vs control); prolonged pair interactions +0.26 occurrences (birdsong); prolonged group interactions +0.19 occurrences (water), each versus the lowest group
